disease_info: Persistent Depressive Disorder (PDD), or dysthymia, is a chronic depressive condition characterized by a low mood lasting at least two years in adults, with accompanying cognitive, emotional, and somatic features that are less intense than major depressive episodes but more enduring. Individuals often describe themselves as having always been this way, and the disorder may be punctuated by superimposed major depressive episodes (“double depression”). Functioning is typically maintained at a basic level, but with significant subjective distress, reduced productivity, and impaired quality of life in work, relationships, and self-care. It is differentiated from major depressive disorder primarily by its chronicity and trait-like course, and from cyclothymia or bipolar disorders by the absence of hypomanic or manic episodes.

narrative.personality: Nicole is a thoughtful, nurturing educator who balances intellectual curiosity with a quiet, longstanding tendency to worry and self-criticize.
narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Nicole was reassigned from her familiar middle-school classroom to a central office curriculum specialist role after district-wide budget cuts and staffing changes she had little control over. Although the move looked like a promotion, she felt disconnected from the daily contact with students that had anchored her sense of purpose, and the increasing demands of district politics, data mandates, and contentious school board meetings left her feeling chronically worn down. Over the next two years she continued to deliver high-quality work and lead mindfulness sessions for colleagues, but she noticed a gradual erosion of her enthusiasm for teaching, found it harder to engage in her usual gardening and book-club routines, and began questioning whether any of her efforts were making a difference in a system she saw as increasingly rigid and unsupportive. She finally sought psychiatric care when a new curriculum cycle loomed, her workload intensified again, and she realized that the persistent low mood and loss of inner drive were now affecting her mentoring relationships and her ability to plan creatively for the coming school year.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just feel down all the time now, like the joy has gone out of my work and my days.”

narrative.personality: Gail is an energetic, competitive organizer who thrives on leading community projects and creative collaborations, but can be perfectionistic and driven by external recognition.
narrative.stressor: Roughly three years ago, Gail’s father—her main cheerleader and frequent companion in genealogical research and community events—died suddenly after a brief illness, just as she was preparing to launch a new arts nonprofit. In the months that followed, she pushed herself to keep running community theatre productions and volunteering, but found that each grant rejection, board conflict, or minor setback felt amplified against the backdrop of his absence and the loss of his steady encouragement. Over the subsequent two years, she gradually withdrew from some leadership roles, struggled to sustain the same intensity in her organizing work, and began to see her carefully laid plans for the nonprofit and her community initiatives as futile, even as others still viewed her as a capable leader. She eventually came to psychiatric care after confiding to a fellow board member that she no longer believed her projects—or her life more broadly—were headed anywhere meaningful, and realizing that this bleak outlook had been quietly deepening and constraining her choices for more than two years.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve started to feel like nothing I do is going to matter and the future just looks pointless.”

narrative.personality: Phillip is a steady, meticulous supervisor who enjoys quiet, nature-focused hobbies and careful planning, sometimes to the point of over-scheduling himself.
narrative.stressor: About two years and a few months ago, Phillip developed a persistent back and shoulder strain after a season of long hours supervising a major expansion in the agricultural operation, which forced him to cut back on some of the physical work he prided himself on and rely more on others for tasks he used to handle himself. The lingering discomfort, multiple medical visits, and advice to limit certain activities made him feel less capable at work and at home, and he slowly stopped going on longer hikes, doing woodworking projects, and volunteering as often for conservation outings. Over time, the combination of ongoing pain, disrupted sleep, and the sense that he could no longer keep up with the demands of both the fields and his own high standards wore him down, and his days began to feel like an exhausting grind despite his attempts to over-plan and compensate. He finally sought psychiatric help after his spouse pointed out that his constant tiredness and disengagement were affecting family life and that he had been in this depleted state for more than two years without improvement despite resolving most of the acute physical injury.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m exhausted all the time, no matter how much I rest, and I just don’t have any energy left for anything.”
